prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, through the conception and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider

statement.case_for: The 2012 observation of the Higgs boson by two independent experiments is the clearest case on this shortlist of a discovery in the sense I weigh most heavily: nature answered a question that the field had carried for half a century, and the answer could in principle have been different. The 2013 prize recognised the theoretical mechanism; the experimental confirmation, which required two of the largest instruments ever built, has not been recognised, and a decade of coupling and spin-parity measurements has only strengthened the result. Maturity is not in doubt. I keep it first because its scientific weight is exceptional and because a committee that honours the theory but never the experiment leaves the record lopsided.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real obstacle, and I do not want to minimise it. Five colleagues put this candidate in their lists and several of them flagged the same problem: the discovery was made by thousands of people, and three founding proposers and leaders are a proxy for collective work, not three discrete acts of discovery. Spokespersons and analysis leaders at the time of discovery have a competing claim, and the credited names exclude them. If the committee cannot defend the trio as representing the decisive contributions, a prize built on it is weaker than the physics deserves. By contrast the optical lattice clock case, now backed by three first-place rankings, has a far cleaner two-person attribution and an equally mature experimental record.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, crediting Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's record accuracy, and notes that the comb and ion-clock work is already recognised so credit separation is relatively clean. She also ranks the Higgs experiment second but doubts that leadership-based attribution is acceptable.
responses.response: I agree that the clock case has the cleaner attribution, and that is a serious strength; I have moved it from outside my top group to a genuine alternative. I disagree that the leadership basis disqualifies the Higgs case: Nobel committees have always had to name three people for collective efforts, and the founding proposers shaped both detectors. But I accept that this is a weaker allocation than Katori and Ye, and that is my main reservation, not a reason to downgrade the science. I do not think a precision-metrology advance, however elegant, answers a question comparable to the origin of mass, and I would say so even though I am not an atomic physicist.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Higgs experiment seventh because its significance is exceptional but the credited names are founding spokespersons or leaders rather than a clean individual-discovery set, and the 2013 prize already acknowledged the discovery in part.
responses.response: I take the attribution point at face value, and it is why I list uncertainties rather than claiming the trio is obvious. I disagree on the 2013 prize: that award went to the theory and says nothing about the observation, which is a separate achievement, as in earlier cases where prediction and detection were recognised separately. Where I would agree with Mehlig is that if the committee finds no defensible three names, the right answer is to turn to another candidate, not to stretch the credit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the Higgs experiment third; he calls the Higgs credit a reasonable if imperfect proxy for experimental leadership, notes that each year of delay tightens the question, and values the kilometre-scale detector as a decades-long achievement.
responses.response: We agree that the Higgs credit is imperfect but defensible, and I find his point about delay persuasive. Where we differ is ordering. IceCube's diffuse flux is a real discovery of the kind I look for, and I rank it second, but source identification is still partial, so the astrophysical interpretation is still developing, whereas the Higgs result is settled. I would still support Halzen and Spiering, and I think the pioneer question for Baikal and DUMAND is manageable with a carefully worded citation. It is a strong alternative but I would not put it ahead of the Higgs.

responses.point: Eriksson places magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene second and topological insulators third, arguing that twisted bilayer graphene offers a tight theory-to-experiment link and that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp's work is confirmed by ARPES and band-structure calculations, while noting the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and 3D pioneers.
responses.response: I share his view that topological insulators are mature and important; I ranked them fifth, below the two discoveries I prefer, mainly because the omitted contributors make the three-person allocation contestable, as he also says. On twisted bilayer graphene I am more cautious than he is: the pairing mechanism is unresolved and the field is still moving quickly, so I would wait. His own point that the interpretation is not fully settled is the argument for patience.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first and trapped-ion and cold-atom quantum computing second, arguing that controlling the light shift so the trap drops out changes what can be measured, and that the redefinition of the second makes recognition natural.
responses.response: This is the argument that most affects my thinking about the clock candidate, because the magic-wavelength idea is simple, original and has delivered a hundredfold improvement in a measurable quantity. I accept that it may be the most defensible two-person configuration on the table. I am less convinced by the framing that the redefinition of the second is pending: the committee should reward what has been achieved, not an event still to come, and he himself lists that as an uncertainty. I would not object strongly if the committee settled on Katori and Ye.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts founding proposers and leaders (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) as a fair representation of the ATLAS and CMS discovery, or insists on spokespersons or analysis leaders at the time of discovery, who are not among the credited names.
Whether the strong clustering of opening first places on optical lattice clocks reflects scientific merit or simply a cleaner, easier-to-defend attribution.
For IceCube, how to word a citation that is fair to Baikal and DUMAND pioneers while naming only Halzen and Spiering.
I am relying on my own knowledge of the history and have not verified individual roles in either collaboration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. I worked at CERN for two years in the early 1990s, before the ATLAS and CMS experiments were built, and my profile shows no connection to Della Negra, Jenni or Virdee; I flag the CERN affiliation only for transparency. My profile does not link me to any other shortlisted candidate or their credited names.
